title: Personal Trainer Red Flags: What Bad Trainers Get Wrong
paragraphs: Miles: So, welcome to another episode of the PT Launch Lab podcast. Today's guest, I'm excited to announce, is Charles Townend. Charles is a successful current PT who's on the floor, in the trenches, doing it day in, day out at a quality gym, Graft House in Leeds. Charles: Graft House in Kirkstall in Leeds, yeah, really great facility. Miles: So I've known Charles a long time. He was a member of one of my gyms many moons ago, and I'm interested for him to tell his story of his journey and to tell us what's really going on 2026. Not what is the smoke and mirrors version, what's the real version of PT on the floor in 2026. So, Charles, tell us a bit about yourself and your journey into PT.

Charles: So, I fell into PT, it was a bit of an accident actually. Um, like most guys, member of a gym for absolutely ages, and um, I ended up having I had a stroke. Uh, I was in really shit shape. You know, we all think- I was that guy who'd go around the gym and I would give people advice. I'd red flags. Oh, you should be doing this, you should be doing this. I'm stood there, I couldn't see my toes. But, you know, trying to give advice thinking I was I was brilliant. Um, I had a stroke, I was 39, and then I hired an online coach. That guy got me into great shape and I started getting some- I started to get noticed on there, then people said to me, why don't you enter a bodybuilding competition?

Charles: Which I did. It was the Miami Pro World Championships. Came 5th in that, and from then I had more of a platform to start giving people advice. Yeah. Then I took my PT qualifications. Unfortunately, I lost my job. And that's when I became a PT at MPfit. Miles: So realistically, the world the world forced you into this career? Charles: Yeah, yeah. Miles: Synchronicity, yeah? Charles: Best thing that could have happened, I think. At the time you think, oh, absolute disaster, but it moulds you. Becoming a PT, it it makes you a better person, and I'll go through that as we chat. Miles: On your journey. Okay, okay. So when you started as a PT, what year was that, do you remember? Charles: About 2016. Miles: Oh, so we're 10 years in then? Charles: Yeah.

Miles: So you've got 10 years of experience you can pull upon on this podcast, so you're not the virgin sex therapist that I've said on another- Charles: No, no, no. Miles: So yeah, so you've got your 10 years experience, you've got your your your your Blue Peter badge for that. Callum: That was my favourite line you ever said. Miles: Yeah, I quite like that one, I quite like that one, yeah. Charles: I'll have to come up with some classics Miles: on Callum: this one. I'm not Miles: up to it right now. So, so, 10 years now, if you were to look at your 10-year journey and we fast forward to 2026, what do you think is the health and the state of the PT industry in 2026?

Charles: It's easy to become a PT. There are probably more PTs than ever, and I would say there are more underqualified, underprepared PTs. That is what I see now. But throughout my entire journey, there's always been a few bad apples. And you look around the gym as a PT and you see these and you think, what are they doing? Um, I think now, PTs are almost the bottom feeders of the health industry. We are taken advantage of massively by people selling us courses. So buy 'em high, sell 'em cheap, you know, kind of thing. It's you know £3,000 for a PT and suddenly, oh, you can earn £50 an hour. So that attracts a certain type of person.

Charles: And we are just, you know, from a from my point of view, we are treated really badly, and that reflects in the quality of the work that we put out. You know, the guys who are the guys who are PTs nowadays, they see these quick courses, become a PT in 8 weeks. Wow, brilliant, what can you learn in 8 weeks? Nothing really. And they're those people that go onto the gym floor, and we should be the first line of health professionals. Callum: I agree.

Charles: But we're not. You know, you look at you've got the state of the NHS and You know, if you've got an obese person or someone like that coming into a a a a a surgery, they should be given the option, right, you can either wait 12 months for a dietitian or we've got we've got 25 PTs here that we approve of, you can go see one of them 3 times a week. That would mean the PTs would have to up their skills to get on that list, and so it would probably shake out the bad ones. And there are an absolute shedload. the bad ones. I see it all the time. Callum: What do you consider a bad PT?

Charles: Right, so why is- you've gotta look at value for money and what you are being paid for, I think. You are being paid to change someone's life, and it's not it's not cheap nowadays. Someone could be paying you like, say, £60 an hour, right? Every minute is a pound, yeah? For that pound, I want To take my client through a journey, I want them to come in, they're overweight, they can't move, you know, they're frightened of the gym, and I want to say to them in a distinct timescale, in 8 weeks' time you will have lost 3 kilos, you will have lost 4 kilos, you'll be able to move. And to do that you need a plan. Charles: And the number of times I see PTs walking around a gym, no plan, making stuff up- Miles: Looking for a machine that's available.

Charles: Yeah, and I've even seen PTs I've seen PTs about to demonstrate an exercise, get down on the floor to demonstrate it, realise the exercise he's just made up on the spur of the moment doesn't work, and stand back up again and show them some stuff. A person is paying you for a for a result, and for any result you need a plan. And I always say to my clients, if you go to a gym and your personal trainer hasn't got a plan, sack him straight away. That's what I'm paying for. You're not paying for an hour of my time, you're paying for my expertise to take you from this to this. And if I haven't got a plan, sack me.

Callum: Yeah, there's two trains of thought with that. This is just my general thesis on this. A good PT- I mean, this is how I do it. I don't consider myself a good PT because that's a label. Charles: But Callum: also, when I have- I have a selection of exercise and variations of exercise. Every time I go into a session, if it's not on paper, it's not a plan. But I know that client's gonna do that day. I've got a recording method of that. So say for instance, again, Miles, when you're talking about picking a machine, if I go to do a squat with a client and the squat rack's busy, I might change it for a goblet squat. Charles: Totally agree. Callum: Yeah. Miles: When the pattern of movement's the same. Charles: Yeah. So you know, squat, hinge, push, pull. Miles: Yeah.

Charles: I totally get that. However, I want to, you know, if I if I go into the gym and I see people, they're the same PT, over and over again, never having any idea. Callum: Like substance and structure.

Charles: And they don't know, you know, what they did last week, what they're gonna do next week. You know, say someone's got 8 clients and each client performs 6, 7 exercises an exercise. You're telling me that client's remembered what they lifted last week, how many reps, how many sets? I don't believe that, because if he was that clever, he wouldn't be a PT. Um, you know, I just find that you need a plan. Um, and and skill set, skill set. One of the one of the my favourite ones is when I've seen a PT's bio, uh fat loss coach, uh fat loss expert, and then they haven't done one nutrition qualification, and you think, well, fat loss is all about a calorie deficit and the psychology of food.

Charles: You're claiming to be a fat loss coach and have done not- you've done nothing since your PT exams to to move your knowledge on. Yeah. And you know, knowledge moves on all the time. You know, we've got new studies, new exercise techniques, and I think, you know, if you've done your PT qualification 10 years ago and haven't done anything since, should you really still be a PT? Because people are asking, you are expecting people to invest in you, so why aren't you investing in yourself? Yourself. You know, why aren't you progressing? Because, you know, somebody, if someone wants to come to you, it's like buying a new car. You want the latest model. If someone wants to come to my gym, they want the latest model.

Charles: model of me, what do you know, what have you learned this week? You've gotta be on the cutting edge. Now, I'm not the world's greatest biomechanics expert, but when it comes to nutrition, my nutrition courses, became a level 5, I've got a level 5 diploma in advanced nutritional science, so and that's cost me about 6,000 quid, because I know that's important to my clients and where they want to be. Yeah. You know, and I do see guys coming in, 18, 19, 20 years old, just interested in flexing the biceps in front of the mirror and showing off to women.

Callum: I mean, ironically, obviously me and Miles are big on investing in yourself as a trainer because we run a provider, but so it's ironic to say, but the aftercare of a personal trainer is a big thing as well. I feel like sometimes they get left to their own devices, whereas the education side is you need to keep going because you're entering a pool of people in this business. And people say PT's saturated. It is, but every business is saturated. The ones that shine through are the ones who are willing to push a little bit further and explore a little bit more, because it can open up doors, right? And personal training, that certificate can mean anything.

Callum: Me personally, it got me into education, you know. It can get people to being gym owners, it can be online coaching, it can be people building systems for it. There's so many avenues where you can go down. But if personal training is what you want to do, you need to try and bring yourself to the best level.

Charles: But again, like I said, the the opportunities- through my nutrition qualification, I now give talks in in businesses, so you know, talk about how to improve the health of the staff, etc. And that's a nice element to it, because if you really want to help people, that's one of the best ways to do it, by standing there giving advice. When you see, when I spoke about a bad PT, when you're about, you know, I want to help people, well, go be in nurse for 6 months because I don't believe you want to help people. You know, help people is a is a really broad statement to make, especially if you're an 18, 19, 20-year-old. You can't even help yourself.

Charles: And that's not me being disrespectful, but what are you bringing to the table to a 35-year-old bloke who runs a business, a 40-year-old with 2 kids? You're not bringing much into that. You've got the qualification to say, I can I can do some bicep curls. But life experience-wise, you've got nothing to offer. I think as a PT, because I was I was talking to Josh earlier on and I said there should be a minimum age requirement almost. Callum: I Charles: can see like, oh no, because maybe not, but you I wouldn't take advice from an 18-year-old on how to do something.

Callum: But if the intention's there, I mean, you're gonna anybody that starts the journey early and they have the intention helping people, which I have met quite a few candidates who do this, is it not they need those milestones of potential failure, which unfortunately some clients are going to suffer that, but they need those to either grow or break? Charles: I still think everyone needs life experience. Callum: Yeah. Charles: You know, it's it's very difficult to advise someone how, you know, to make changes to their life if you haven't made changes to your own. You know, how can you say, oh, like, I'm an expert fat loss coach if I haven't lost a bit of fat?

Miles: What about looking at this another way? We we we think spin the whole thing on its head. So there's there's there's the age in isolation, but there's the walking a mile in someone's shoes in isolation. Because somebody could be, for example, 21, But has done a dramatic body transformation. They might not have the age, but they've they've done the journey. Charles: Yeah. Well, yeah, I do agree with that. Um, I do think if you're coaching something, regardless of the age, you do need to have done it. Miles: Yeah. Charles: And you need to have done it uh well. Callum: Back what you say.

Charles: Um, because you know, I've you know, I've I've gone from being overweight to a I ended up winning a Mr. Universe title, right? So I know how to build an elite physique, so I can I can coach that. But I can't coach some well I have coached going to a high rocks, but not to a high level because I've never done one and it's not my thing. But if you you have to have done what you claim you can coach doing, I believe. Miles: I agree with that.

Charles: But you know, that could come with life experience as well. So if if I'm teaching a 35-year-old The circles merge. Yeah, if I teach a 35-year-old guy to lose weight, I've also gotta be able to think, ah, as a 35-year-old guy, I've got 2 kids, I've got a wife who's not gonna want to be in every weekend when I want to be eating chicken and rice, she's gonna want to go out. You've gotta be able to to marry those. I think the personal training qualification, the ones I did, are very A, B, black, white. Miles: Yeah, like a driving test. Yeah, teaches you the bare basics of driving. Charles: I'm glad you said that because just because you've got a driving licence doesn't mean you should be on the road. Callum: I love that quote! I say it all the time. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah,

Charles: yeah. Just because you've just because you've qualified as a PT does not mean you should be on the road. Callum: Say it all the time. Absolutely, I agree with that. No, no, no, that's fantastic. I feel like you just read my mind. Miles: Yeah, we we we talk about that a lot. Yeah, we talk about that a lot. Charles: Yeah, but you see it all the time. Miles: Yes, yeah, you think, how was that person even on the road? Charles: Yeah. Miles: But technically they've passed The driving test. Charles: You know, the same in gyms again, on about poor PTs. I've seen PTs actually physically join in with a client's session. Yeah. And I'm thinking- Miles: While eating Tupperware. Charles: I was gonna mention, I was gonna- Miles: Let's not go there, let's not go there, let's not go there. Callum: We like to talk about specific things. Miles: Let's not go there.

Charles: Well, I I I've seen that, people shuffling off to the kitchen to grab grab their breakfast and eat eat the breakfast whilst someone's doing burpees. Miles: Back turned going, "2 more, 2 more," eating out of Tupperware, doing this. Charles: You know this, you know, again, someone's paying you money for that hour. Miles: Yeah. Charles: And your attention should be on them. Callum: Yeah. Miles: I go around gyms all over the country. I've been around, every week I go to different gyms, and when I'm in a gym, I'm always looking at what's the PTs doing, what's the staff doing, what's the standards, what, I'm looking at everything, observing everything. And the amount of times I see PTs Either not engaged, not watching every mechanic, every the tempo, everything about the rep, and just, "Yeah, 2 more." Charles: Hands in pockets. Miles: Hands in pockets, arms folded, not writing down, not tracking.

Charles: I'm old school, pen and pad. Miles: I'm pen and pad. I know some people use iPads and phones, but some of the PTs I see with phones, I genuinely think it's Tinder. I don't think they're tracking the session because they're not looking at what the client's doing and they're almost just WhatsApping or doing- Charles: Yeah. Miles: And the standard of that, that is that is the one thing that still is my pet peeve. Like you said, when you're with that client and you're not with the client, you're not engaged, you're not living and breathing the rep, the session, and you're on your phone or just looking around. Charles: Looking around, I can't be bothered with this. I really can't, yeah, I see that quite often.

Miles: I would I would say if you were somebody looking at picking a PT in a gym, whatever gym in the country or the world you're in, if you're on the treadmill watching somebody delivering a session, I would say when you said when we said what's what is a bad PT, that for me is number 1. Not engaged, not paying attention, not watching, not coaching, not being enthusiastic. Charles: Yeah, that is that is the enthusiasm thing. It's like, oh, I just can't, why am I even here today? Callum: Yeah. Charles: And you think, it's almost like some coaches, I used this phrase earlier on, are stealing a living. Yeah, no, it's true. I wouldn't even say the coaches, you know, they are just rep counters. Miles: Rent-a-friend.

Charles: Yeah, you know, as well as that, you know, rent-a-friend does come into it, but you're looking, you think, wow, they are paying you, you know, 30, 40 quid for that. It's quite a highly paid service. service, and maybe you're not delivering what you should be doing.

Callum: Yeah, I mean, it's a problem because, like driving licences, they give PT certificates out all the time, and it doesn't come with the preference that- what you said before about PT should have been at the front line of health. And there's a lot of responsibility with this, and I do this every time I'm assessing a client and I look at the programme that they had submitted to me. If the first thing it says on it is a deadlift I want to have a conversation to make sure they understand the deadlift. Because these exercises can be dangerous. You're putting someone in vulnerable positions, and if you don't know what you're doing but you've seen it online, I can't trust you to do that.

Callum: And I'm not taking away from anyone's intelligence. I'm saying I've been there myself, but I've hurt myself on these exercises. There's a lot of responsibility. If you're not paying attention, if you're not present, if you're not doing it, if you've not got a reason for doing it. There's a lot of potential risk that they're gonna leave way worse than they came in. And yeah, it's, it's a pet peeve, but I can also understand why they're doing it, because no one's saying to them, you need to do better than this. Because from the outside in, PT looks attractive. If you're someone who loves the gym and you're there all the time, and someone says to you, why don't you just start training people, make some money out Charles: of it? Yeah, yeah.

Callum: It's like, oh yeah, it's a lightbulb moment, everyone's gonna be Queuing outside the door because Johnny Big Biceps is in the gym all the time. It's like, yeah, everyone's gonna listen to me. And then you realise pretty suddenly there's a lot more to it than looking great. It's also being able to talk to people, understand people, emotionally connect with people. You know, like we said, half the time it's about being a therapist and half the time it's about connecting with people. You might spend a full hour and a half session doing 3 exercises. Charles: I I did that today. Callum: Yeah. Charles: Literally an hour and a half with someone just chatting about the business. And that's fine. But I I I said to someone else again today- I did a lot of talking about this today, didn't I? Callum: A lot of prep.

Charles: Yeah. Can you tell? Lily's shaking away in the corner. I I want my client to leave the gym feeling better than when they walked in. That doesn't necessarily mean, you know, they can lift any more weight. I just want them to feel better. You know, they they might leave the gym and I'll be thinking, "Every single lift you did today was worse than last time." Right? I'm not gonna tell them that. They you know, how because when as we finish the last exercise, I will say to them, "How do you feel?" "Brilliant, I feel better than I walked in." That's all I need to hear. Yes, I know you've done everything correctly, you haven't injured yourself, we've talked about some food, you know, we've pointed out, "Oh, you actually got a bit stronger on that exercise, have you noticed?" "Oh, that's brilliant, yeah, I feel a lot stronger now." Yeah.

Charles: But as long as- my demographic is menopausal women, so they're not after, you know, chasing big biceps and huge squat numbers. They just want to stop falling over and look better naked, right? If I'm pushing them on that road, because you know it's gonna take longer than a younger person, that's fine. But be aware of what you're selling. Callum: Yeah. Charles: And sell it well. Miles: So how do you- so that's your- that's your demographic now. Charles: Yeah. Miles: Yeah. How do you manage expectations of that that client category? Because like you said, that can be that coaching that client category can come with challenges, because results might not be as fast.

Charles: Well, they're not as fast, but also they're not as apparent. You know, they're not as they're never gonna get into, you know, the skimpy dress of an 18 and 19-year-old, and you've gotta set set different targets. I think, you know, so it's not always about losing weight, it's about have you got a little bit stronger. Um, you know, and that I think, once you've set your targets, it's easy for them to to realise they are making progress. So it's, that is the way you'd you'd manage that. Miles: Yeah. Charles: That, I'm I right, when you come in, I am not expecting you to lose 10 kilos in 10 weeks, right? Miles: Yeah.

Charles: I would like you to be able to do this and that, and this and that, and this and that. Oh, and it just seems so far away from them, right? But after 3 weeks, they're already thinking, "Oh my god, I've nearly reached my 10-week target. That's fantastic." Or, "I'll start to think maybe about a bit of weight loss now, and maybe about toning up a little bit." Because the word toning, I do believe, is a thing for my demographic, you know, because that's what they want to do. Um, just don't set lofty targets. So they'll look around the gym and they'll see the 18 and 19-year-olds in the figure-hugging shorts. And it's like, yeah, but you know, that's not for you.

Charles: And it's it might be a little bit demoralising for them, but then they kind of come to, actually, no, that isn't for me. I just want to feel better. Yeah. You know, I had a client today, we haven't done TRX rows for 6, 8 months. She did them today, she went, "Oh my god, I feel stronger on that." And she says, "I was in the shower and I like, I've got..." Miles: I know, it's starting back

Charles: in my arms, yeah, yeah, yeah. And one of them said, oh, she's got tons of... So you don't have to sell it to them and just and and explain that these you know the criteria set originally originally had been met. They will tell you it's like, "Oh my god." This and the other thing that's a really great one is, I'll film them doing an exercise and then show them the video and I'll say, "And if you'd seen that on Instagram, you'd say, 'Wow, that's great.' But guess what? That actually is you." And they're like, "Oh, that's amazing." You just need to you know get the right lighting, a little bit of muscle, it's like, "Yeah, do you know what?" I'm sold on this. Miles: Yeah, yeah.

Callum: I think it's the framing in it, because especially with the clients that come in nowadays, because they've got so much exposure to social media, their expectations of what their goals are is much different from what the expectation- what they actually want. And yeah, when a client comes in, it's like, I want to lose X amount of weight, I want to improve my figure, I want to do this, I want to do that. It's like, well, why? Like, you need to ask why, because if you're not asking why, you don't actually know what your goal is. Charles: Yeah.

Callum: And there's gonna be a point where you dip and you don't know actually, you know, what you want. Is it- are you progressing? Are you not? Are you- is it worth it? If you haven't got the actual goal you want in mind, then it's not gonna prophesy itself, you're not gonna come forward. Um, yeah, and I agree with that as well, trying to find those little wins, making sure they actually understand it's a lifestyle. I think that's really hard for PTs to do now, is to sell their services, because everyone lives in 8-week packages. Charles: Yeah. Callum: You know, get fit in 60, do this, and because- Charles: Make a photo shoot.

Callum: Yeah, and don't get me wrong, I know it sells, but no one's considering this as a factor. What happens when they achieve that goal? What's next? Is there a next point? Have you got an aftercare plan? Have you got something to talk to them about? Because if people want to live here and now really quick, they're not understanding the value of why people enjoy going to the gym in the first place. I think that is a really tough selling point. I think we talked to Josh about like how you communicate your services online, it's getting ever more difficult to be a genuine person because coaches are now seeing what other people are doing online and copying and role modelling and not being themselves.

Charles: The good thing about a lot of my demographic is that, say the 40, 45, 50, right, their parents are in their 80s and they are they had they're those 80-year-olds weren't exposed to the same amount of social media that we are now, so they weren't aware of of what fitness was and how to stay fit. So they're struggling to stand up, sit down, carry the shopping. And I can say to them, you don't want to end up like your parents. My dad's in that 80-year-old range and I can see he's struggling to walk. And you think, wow, you know, this is not great. And they will see their their elders struggling and they don't want to be like that.

Charles: I kept some of my clients for 7 or 8 years because they can see the value going forward. You know, they haven't had the most amazing body transformations, and that for me is a little bit disappointing. You think, oh, I see all these other coaches having body transformations. Then you think to yourself, but that's not my market. You know, my market is taking someone who wants to have a great life at 40, 50, 60, 70, and can and can still wipe their own backsides at 80. And when you say that, originally they're like, oh yeah. And then they see that the I say the parents, struggling to think, and the the the lightbulb moment, the penny drops, like, "Oh my god, yeah, actually I want to be strong.

Charles: I get it now." Yeah. So I don't I don't have to have massive wins every week. I'm just not getting, sounds bad, any worse. Callum: Yeah, you're accumulating. Miles: Yeah, yeah, yeah, you want that person to have their independence, to be able to get out of the bath. Charles: Yes. Miles: Off the toilet, not fall.

Charles: And this does age. But this doesn't resonate with a with a young PT. I'm going back to them because all they think about is, you know, biceps, chest, big great physique, great glutes. Yeah. They're not thinking about the 50-year-old who just wants to be able to get out of a chair. In fact, I had a client today say to me, she said, "I remember when getting out of a chair was..." She sat down on a bench and she struggled to get off. Then she says, "Now look at this." And she sat down on stuff, she says, "I can do that now." Callum: Mm-hmm, Charles: yeah. And you know, when she came in to see me 2 years ago, she was brought in by a friend and she was like, "I really don't want to I come." don't need the KT, I don't want to train. And then it was like, I get it.

Callum: Yeah, it's a life experience thing. Like, as an example, I didn't appreciate 8 hours sleep until I had a child. Charles: Right, okay. Callum: I I was like, I can I can take whatever sleep I want, I can still function every day. If I get less than 6 hours sleep, I am a nightmare because I've got a child to look after. And I realise how valuable sleep is. And the relationship I'm making is life experiences teach you. It teaches you. Like, if you've got an 18-year-old PT who's training someone in their 40s, for instance, you know, and they're they're struggling between sets and like, oh, we've got 12 sets to complete today, we're gonna do this. That person only does 6, they think it's a failure. They're happy they just made it.

Charles: Yeah. You've gotta be able to, I think, be uh when I said it made you a better person, if you work in an office, you really don't have many people to deal with, but when When someone comes into the gym, you are you are like a sponge for all their emotions and you you learn how to just just morph into a different person on every session, you know. This person doesn't want to talk, this person does. This person has, you know, maybe depressive moments, this person doesn't have a good relationship with food. And you you get so much more. Callum: Ryan calls it being a chameleon. Charles: Yeah, exactly, yeah, yeah, you are a chameleon. Miles: Well, you're different personality types, as we know, that some people you need to be very direct with. Charles: Yes.

Miles: Some people you need to be very empathetic with, because to get the most out of that client in that session on their journey, you know the ones you need to give them a real push and the ones you need to be a bit softly softly with. Charles: I don't know if I should say this, but I've actually sacked two clients mid-session because of what they were saying. Just like, do you know what, actually, you've had loads of this, I've been with you for 18 months and what you're just telling me now is absolutely It's absolute bullshit, and I know it's a lie, and I've actually said, look, session stops there. Miles: It's not good for me, it's not good for you, it's not working.

Charles: Yeah, it's a waste of your money. PT is not cheap, and this is a real drain on me. I had a client one time, she came in and she was complaining, and she stopped mid-complain and said, I need to stop doing this because you've probably had about 8 of these today. So as well as you take the good energy on, Callum: Yeah. Charles: You take all that on, it's like you don't realise it, but it just whittles you down a little bit.

Callum: Yeah, I think it takes a certain amount of time when you first start with a client who's been very new to the gym. Their first motivation is punishment because they want to come in saying, I need to change because I hate the way I look. And you, your job as a trainer is to switch that narrative, reverse engineer it, and say, I'm coming to the gym because I love being here, and your body changes as a byproduct. That's like the last thing that changes, your mind first, body. But some people get stuck in that rhythm of that punishment life. So when you're asking them to do something like, let's go do some squats, like, I hate squats, I hate this, and like, you're leaving that negativity.

faqs.q: What makes a bad personal trainer?
faqs.a: Charles points to trainers with no plan who make sessions up as they go, and to trainers who aren't paying attention: on their phone, hands in pockets, or eating while the client works. Miles says being disengaged is the number one sign. Charles also calls out PTs who market themselves as fat loss experts without any nutrition qualification.

faqs.q: Does qualifying as a PT mean you are ready for the gym floor?
faqs.a: Not on its own. Charles compares it to a driving test: "just because you've got a driving licence doesn't mean you should be on the road." The qualification teaches the basics; life experience, a plan for each client and the ability to read people are what make a trainer good.

faqs.q: How do you manage expectations with older clients?
faqs.a: Charles works mainly with menopausal women and sets targets beyond the scales: getting stronger, moving better, getting out of a chair without struggling. Small, reachable targets mean clients see progress within weeks, and he has kept some clients for seven or eight years.

faqs.q: What would Charles do if he started as a PT from scratch?
faqs.a: Pick a niche and stick to it, put your personality on social media so people know you as a person, start building your Instagram while you are still qualifying, and be visible on the gym floor by talking to everyone.

faqs.q: Should personal trainers get involved in online arguments?
faqs.a: Charles's advice is not to comment in the first place. Arguments rarely reach your clients and just waste your time. If you want to change someone's mind, take it into DMs, where the conversation might even turn into a client.

faqs.q: Should coaches use AI for client check-ins?
faqs.a: Charles calls it "bang out of order". AI can help you start something like a basic meal plan, but it can be wrong, so you need to know your stuff and adjust it yourself. Check-ins are what the client is paying a human coach for.

faqs.q: Is online coaching better than in-person personal training?
faqs.a: Charles thinks online can get better results because you can give a client more work between check-ins, while in-person results are limited by how many sessions a client can afford. Either way, the client has to apply it. He and Miles also warn that the barrier to entry for online coaching is very low.
